title: Home Depot's AI bot helps shoppers avoid the dreaded second trip
excerpt: The Home Depot was one of the first major retailers to deliver a customer-facing AI bot that can help tackle complex DIY projects.
content_html:
By Dominick Reuter

You're currently following this author! Click to unsubscribe from email alerts.

2026-11-20T15:43:56.764Z

If there's one frustration many DIYers experience, it's the sudden realization that you brought home the wrong supplies for the job. It's a problem Home Depot is hoping to solve with AI.

The home improvement giant originally built its early reputation in part on knowledgeable store associates, including plumbers, electricians, and other tradespeople who could help do-it-yourself customers. Now, with AI, the company is trying to put that project-based know-how right into consumers' hands.

The company was one of the first major retailers to deliver a customer-facing AI bot, called Magic Apron. The platform was specifically trained on products and projects that Home Depot has loaded into the tool over the past two years, so it can serve as an advisor to shoppers.

"What's important for our customers is the project and not the product," Rebecca Godecke, president of Home Depot's online division, said in an interview. "I think it's really easy to do single-item selling, but that's actually not what we think AI is best suited for."

Godecke said she was recently with a shopper who had loaded her cart with a replacement toilet and other items for the project. They used Magic Apron to snap a photo of the cart's contents to make sure they had everything, and it delivered a helpful warning.

"Magic Apron was able to identify that and say, 'You have an incompatible wax ring. You need to go back to this aisle and try again,'" Godecke said.

"The last thing you want is you've taken off the old toilet, and you're about to put the new one on and you figure out that, 'Oh, I've got the wrong wax ring!'" she added. "That's a terrible conundrum to be in."

Home Depot's journey with its AI assistant was an evolution to add more and more capabilities.

When it first launched, Home Depot began by putting its know-how into a chatbot on its website. In March 2025, the assistant made a public introduction in the company's app and on millions of product pages. The app could answer product questions, summarize reviews, and give some how-to guidance.

At a December 2025 investor meeting, a Home Depot executive said the app was beginning to move away from just answering questions and that the company was using the AI tool to build shopping carts for customers. The next month, the company expanded its partnership with Google to extend the app's AI capabilities.

After testing in stores, the company rolled out in-store capability in August tailored to each of Home Depot's 2,000-plus locations, so that the assistant could guide shoppers to the inventory and layout of a particular store. It can also detect and communicate in multiple languages.

As consumers have been using AI more in their own lives, shopping assistants are fast becoming a must-have for major retailers, including Walmart's Sparky, Amazon's Alexa, and Target's Ask Target. Walmart and Target both said this week that customer adoption of their AI agents is growing fast.

Home improvement rival Lowe's has Mylow, which was developed in collaboration with OpenAI and serves functions similar to Magic Apron. Lowe's CEO Marvin Ellison said Wednesday that MyLow answers over a million questions per month and that users have a conversion rate three times that of non-users shopping online.

Godecke said Magic Apron now fields millions of questions per month, and they're often about DIY projects that go well beyond simply finding a single item.

Employees are also using Magic Apron to help shoppers complete projects that might extend beyond their specialties, she said. For example, a garden center associate may know a lot about plants, but feel less confident about exterior lighting.

By solving for an entire project, she said the Magic Apron tool is leading to more complete shopping carts that get it right the first time. And that translates to fewer return trips to replace or return improper items.

"What we're seeing is that as you use it once and you're familiar with it, you come back and use it more," Godecke said.

Dominick Reuter
